title: How interest works, simply
description: Interest can help savings grow or make borrowing cost more — here is the idea in plain language.

body.heading: Interest when you save
paragraphs: When you keep money in a savings account, the bank may pay you interest — a small extra amount — for keeping it there. If you save $100 and the interest for a year is 2%, you would have about $102 after a year, before any fees or tax.
Over time, you can also earn interest on the interest you already earned. That snowball idea is called compound interest, and it is why starting early, even with small amounts, can help.

body.heading: Interest when you borrow
paragraphs: Borrowing works the other way. If you borrow money, interest is part of what you pay back on top of the amount borrowed. Borrowing $100 at 20% interest for a year could mean paying back about $120 if nothing is repaid during that year.
That is why reading the interest rate and the total cost matters before borrowing. A low monthly payment can still mean a high total cost if it stretches over a long time.

body.heading: No promises, just maths
paragraphs: Interest rates change, accounts have different rules, and this article is education only — not a recommendation for any account or loan. The lasting lesson is simple: interest rewards patience when you save, and adds cost when you borrow.

takeaway: Interest is a small percentage with big effects over time — in your favour when saving, against you when borrowing.
